title: Analysing Student Talk in Whole-Class Teaching esearchgate.net/publication/336770155_Analysing_student_talk_moves_in_whole_class_teaching
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 17, 2024 — original paper: https://www.r
summary: This page summarizes Jan Hardman's discourse-analytical framework for examining student talk during whole-class teaching, built to distinguish brief responses from extended, dialogic contributions. Hardman applies the framework to lesson transcripts from a professional-development program designed to promote dialogic teaching, comparing intervention schools against controls. Students in intervention schools produced significantly richer and more dialogic talk, marked by more argumentation, justification, and elaboration than their peers in control schools. Barton's summary frames extended student contributions as a key quality indicator for a classroom: the more students argue, justify, and elaborate rather than just answer briefly, the deeper the thinking likely taking place. The paper's practical suggestion is that teachers broaden their questioning repertoire toward open-ended questions, probe for evidence, and deliberately build student answers into subsequent questions to create thematic coherence across a lesson's dialogue.
points: Extended student contributions — argumentation, justification, elaboration — are proposed as a key indicator of classroom quality, not just a nice-to-have.
Teachers who broaden their questioning toward open-ended prompts, probe for evidence, and build student answers into follow-up questions produce measurably richer dialogic talk.

A professional-development program aimed at dialogic teaching produced significantly more argumentation and elaboration in intervention schools compared to controls, suggesting the skill is trainable.
Reflecting on and reviewing your own lessons is highlighted as a practical way for teachers to improve the quality of classroom talk they are eliciting.
